title.title: Existential real sentences in the counting hierarchy
title.subtitle: Claim: the existential theory of the reals lies in $\mathsf C_{26}\mathsf P$, a fixed level of the counting hierarchy

plain: Deciding whether polynomial equations have a real solution is easier than known: it comes down to counting

beats.text: Schematically: $\exists\mathbb{R}$ was known to sit inside PSPACE (Canny, 1988)
Graph drawing, 3-player Nash and training feasibility are $\exists\mathbb{R}$-complete
Claimed: all of it fits inside the counting hierarchy, at level 26

steps: Turn the question into a polynomial hitting zero
A good choice sits at roots of polynomials we can find
Give each needed root a short label
Guess the labels and check them by counting

achievement.label: Is the existential theory of the reals in CH? (open)
achievement.context: Before: $\exists\mathbb{R} \subseteq$ PSPACE (Canny, 1988); PosSLP in CH (Allender et al., 2009)

verify.ourCheck: We did not referee the proof; nothing here is machine-checked

voice.text: Graph drawing and network training reduce to real equations. The bound was polynomial space.
Roots get short labels, which are guessed and checked by counting.
Claimed: inside the counting hierarchy, level twenty six.

sources.quote: in particular ETR (and all of exists-R) lies in C_26 P
Whether exists-R lies in CH (or below PSPACE) was a known open question
graph drawing, Nash with 3 players, neural net training feasibility
Level 26 of the counting hierarchy is a structural result, not an algorithm; unformalized.
